title: The Gentiles too
sum: News of Cornelius reaches Jerusalem before Peter does, and when he arrives some believers take him to task: he went into a Gentile house and ate there. Peter answers by telling the whole story in order, from the sheet let down from heaven to the Spirit falling on the Gentiles "the same way he fell on us in the beginning." If God gave them the same gift, who was Peter to stop God? His critics fall silent and then praise God: even the Gentiles have been given repentance that brings life.

Luke then turns north. Believers scattered after Stephen's death reach Antioch in Syria, and some unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene begin telling Greek-speaking Gentiles about the Lord Jesus. A large church grows. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who rejoices, encourages them, and fetches Saul from Tarsus to help teach. It is in Antioch that the disciples are first called "Christians." When a prophet foretells famine, this young church sends relief to the believers in Judea by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
readings: Read as history

Antioch, the capital of Roman Syria and home to a large Jewish community that already drew many Greeks to its worship (Josephus, Jewish War 7.45), is exactly where a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles might first take shape. The famine under Claudius, Agrippa's reign and the name "Christians" all fit what other sources tell us of the 40s AD. Historians debate how this visit of Barnabas and Saul to Jerusalem relates to the ones Paul himself describes in Galatians 1–2 (see the deep dive below).
Read as a turning point in the story

Jesus' outline in 1:8 moves from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria to the ends of the earth. Chapter 11 is where the hinge turns. The church in Jerusalem accepts what God did in Caesarea, and the center of the story begins to shift to Antioch, the base for Paul's journeys. From here Luke's camera follows Barnabas and Saul, and soon Paul alone.
Read as a story of the church learning

The apostles do not plan the Gentile mission. God acts first (the vision, the Spirit falling), and the church then remembers Jesus' words and catches up. Peter's critics change their minds when they hear what God has done. Barnabas "saw the grace of God" and rejoiced. Many readers find here a model for how churches should face something new: tell the whole story, test it against Jesus' words, and look for the Spirit's work.

views.H: The first church with many Gentile members grew in Antioch, the third city of the empire, in the late 30s or early 40s. Luke's report that the name "Christians" began there is widely accepted; the Latin ending suggests to many that it came from outsiders or officials, though some think the believers chose it. The famine of Claudius' reign is well attested, most severely in Judea about AD 46–48 (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 20.51–53, 101). Relief from Antioch to Jerusalem fits Paul's own memory of being asked to keep the poor in mind (Galatians 2:10).
views.C: Critical scholars ask how Luke's sequence fits Paul's letters. Paul mentions only two Jerusalem visits before writing Galatians (Galatians 1:18; 2:1); Acts has three by chapter 15. Some think the famine visit (11:30; 12:25) is a doublet of the council visit or Luke's own construction; others identify it with Galatians 2:1–10 (Ramsay, Bruce, Longenecker). The repeated Cornelius story is often seen as Luke's composition, with the speech summarizing the earlier narrative.
views.L: The chapter repeats chapter 10 from Peter's point of view, a technique Luke uses for the events he most wants remembered (compare the three accounts of Paul's call). Two narratives are then woven: Jerusalem accepting Gentile believers (11:1–18), and the Antioch church that will send Paul (11:19–30). The famine relief frames chapter 12: Barnabas and Saul go to Jerusalem at 11:30 and come back at 12:25.
views.J: The dispute in 11:2–3 is a real question of Jewish practice: may a Jew eat at a Gentile's table? Jews of the time answered it in different ways (see the note at 11:3). Luke does not say the Jerusalem believers stopped keeping the Law; later they are "all of them, zealous for the law" (21:20). Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen point out that welcoming Gentiles as Gentiles, without conversion, fits Jewish hopes that the nations would turn to Israel's God at the end of days (Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23).
views.T: The fathers saw in 11:18 the moment the church recognized that salvation was for all nations. Chrysostom praised Peter's humility in giving an account to those under him, and Barnabas as the model of a gentle overseer who rejoices at others' work. The name "Christian" from Antioch became the church's pride: Ignatius of Antioch, martyred about AD 110, wrote that he wished not only to be called a Christian but to be found one.

deep.b:
Until now the believers were Jews, Samaritans and a few God-fearers like the Ethiopian official and Cornelius. At Antioch, for the first time, a whole congregation grows up in which Jews and Gentiles believe side by side, and nobody tells the Gentiles they must first become Jews. Luke gives the credit to unnamed believers from Cyprus and Cyrene (11:20), not to an apostle.

The leadership list in 13:1 shows how varied this church was: a Levite from Cyprus, a man nicknamed "Black," a North African, a man raised at Herod's court, and a former Pharisee from Tarsus. Antioch sends famine relief to Jerusalem (11:29–30), sends Barnabas and Saul to the nations (13:1–3), receives their report (14:26–28), and is where the crisis over circumcision and table fellowship breaks out (15:1–2; Galatians 2:11–14). Much of the rest of Acts begins here.

deep.h: Paul's visits to Jerusalem: Acts and Galatians
deep.b:
Paul swears in Galatians that after his call he did not go up to Jerusalem for three years, then stayed with Peter fifteen days, and went up again fourteen years later with Barnabas and Titus, because of a revelation (Galatians 1:18–2:2). Acts reports these visits up to the council:

  • 9:26–30: after his escape from Damascus. Almost all agree this is Galatians 1:18.
  • 11:30 and 12:25: the famine visit with Barnabas.
  • 15:2–30: the council about circumcision.

Which one is Galatians 2:1–10? (1) Most scholars say the council (Acts 15): the same people, the same issue, the same outcome. They explain Paul's silence about the famine visit in various ways, or doubt that it happened as Luke tells it. (2) Others, following William Ramsay, say the famine visit: Paul's "revelation" could be Agabus' prophecy, the request to keep the poor in mind fits a relief trip, and Galatians never mentions the council's decision, which would have settled the Galatian dispute. On this view Galatians was written before Acts 15, perhaps the earliest of Paul's letters. Both views are held by careful scholars; see also the notes on 11:30 and 15:2.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a name born of the collection?
deep.b: Luke reports the name "Christians" (11:26) right before the famine relief (11:27–30), and the order may not be accidental. Ancient cities watched closely when a group raised money to send abroad; Rome had long had to rule on whether Jewish communities could send their temple tax to Jerusalem. A new association in Antioch collecting funds for people in Judea, under a leader called Christos, would be exactly the kind of group a city official had to name and register. The Latin-style ending fits an official label. This is my suggestion only. It builds on the widely held view that the name came from outsiders. Elias Bickerman argued the opposite: the active verb chrēmatisai means the disciples styled themselves "Christians," taking the name up themselves ("The Name of Christians," 1949). If he is right, this theory falls. No ancient source connects the name with the collection.

echoes: 10:1–48; 15:7–11; 8:1–4; 1:5; 1:8; 2:1–4; Leviticus 11:1–47; Genesis 1:24–30; Matthew 3:11; Luke 3:16; Galatians 1:18–2:14; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–27

settings.what: Peter's defense before the Jerusalem believers
settings.to: the apostles and the believers in Jerusalem, especially "the people of the circumcision" who objected that he had eaten with uncircumcised men
settings.when: on Peter's return from Caesarea, after Cornelius' household received the Spirit and was baptized (10:44–48)
settings.why: Peter does not argue from Scripture or from his authority as an apostle. He tells what happened, step by step, with six witnesses beside him, and ends with Jesus' own promise of the Spirit. The point is to show his critics that the decision was God's, not his: "Did I have the power to stop God?" It works; they fall silent and praise God (11:18). The dispute was about table fellowship, a real question of Jewish practice, not about whether Gentiles could be saved at all.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, this speech answered a question many of them lived with: why does our church welcome Gentiles without making them Jews? Because God did it first, and the apostles in Jerusalem agreed.

settings.to: God, in praise, and to one another
settings.why: Their short confession is the first time the Jerusalem church as a whole accepts that God offers repentance and life to Gentiles. Luke records it as praise, not grudging permission.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learn that the Gentile mission had Jerusalem's blessing from the start, even if the details (circumcision, food) were still to be worked out in chapter 15.

settings.by: Barnabas, sent by the Jerusalem church
settings.to: the new believers at Antioch, Jews and Gentiles
settings.why: Sent to inspect, Barnabas instead encourages: he urges them to stay close to the Lord. His approval tied the young church to Jerusalem without placing new conditions on its Gentile members.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers Barnabas is a model of leadership that recognizes God's work in unexpected places.

settings.to: the church at Antioch, gathered together
settings.when: in the early or middle 40s, during the reign of Claudius (AD 41–54)
settings.why: The prophecy warned of famine so that the church could act ahead of time. Its effect was generosity: the Antioch believers sent relief to Judea. Prophecy in Acts guides the church's practical decisions, as it will again for Paul (21:10–14).
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw that the bond between the Gentile churches and Jerusalem was one of love and shared goods from the beginning, as in Paul's later collection (Romans 15:25–27).

title: A king against the church
sum: King Herod Agrippa I turns on the church. He has James, the brother of John, executed with the sword, the first of the Twelve to die, and when this pleases the crowds he arrests Peter too, at the Passover, under a guard of sixteen soldiers. The church prays without letting up. On the night before Peter's trial an angel wakes him, the chains fall off, gates open by themselves, and Peter finds himself alone in the street. He goes to the house of Mary, John Mark's mother, where the praying church cannot believe the slave girl Rhoda when she says he is at the gate.

Peter leaves Jerusalem, and Herod has the guards led away. Later, at Caesarea, Herod makes a speech in royal robes, the crowd shouts that he is a god, and an angel of the Lord strikes him because he did not give the glory to God; he dies eaten by worms. Josephus tells the same death. "But the word of God kept growing and multiplying." Barnabas and Saul complete their relief mission and return with John Mark.
readings: Read as history

Herod Agrippa I ruled Judea from AD 41 to 44, and Josephus confirms both his eagerness to please the people of Jerusalem and his sudden death at Caesarea after being hailed as a god (Jewish Antiquities 19.343–350). James' execution and Peter's arrest fit a king courting popularity. The escape itself is told as a miracle; historians who do not accept miracles look for other explanations, while others take Luke's account as it stands.
Read as a pattern of passion and rescue

Peter's arrest at Passover under a Herod, the church's earnest prayer, the night, the angel, the woman who first brings the news and is not believed: many readers see Luke shaping Peter's story after Jesus' death and resurrection. James dies as his Master did; Peter, this time, is rescued. The disciple walks the Lord's road.
Read as two kings

The chapter opens with Herod stretching out his hands against the church and closes with Herod struck down, while the word of God grows. An angel "strikes" Peter to wake him and "strikes" Herod to kill him. The contrast is between a king who accepts worship and a God who will not share his glory, and between the power of the sword and the power of prayer.

views.H: Agrippa I, raised in Rome with the imperial family, was king of the Jews AD 41–44 and the last to rule the whole of Herod the Great's kingdom. His death in AD 44 is one of the few fixed dates in Acts. Luke and Josephus agree on the setting (Caesarea), the royal robes, the acclamation as a god and a sudden fatal illness, while differing in details, which suggests two independent reports of one event.
views.C: Critics note that the chapter is built from traditions about Peter, perhaps from Mark's family circle (12:12), and that the escape has features of a common ancient story-type, the miraculous prison escape (compare Euripides' Bacchae and Acts 5:19; 16:26). Opinions differ on how much is history. The order of events is also debated: Agrippa died in 44, while the famine visit of 11:30 may be later (about 46), so Luke may have placed the Herod story inside the visit for literary reasons.
views.L: Luke frames the chapter with the famine visit (11:30; 12:25) and ends it with a summary of growth (12:24). It is the last scene of Peter's leadership; after this the story belongs to Paul, and Peter appears only once more (15:7–11). Comic touches (Rhoda leaving Peter at the gate, the praying church that will not believe) sit beside horror (Herod's death), a mix ancient readers enjoyed.
views.J: "The Jews" in 12:3 and 12:11 are the people and leaders of Jerusalem whom Agrippa wanted to please. Josephus presents Agrippa as a pious king, and the Mishnah remembers a King Agrippa weeping when he read Deuteronomy's law of the king and the people crying, "You are our brother" (Mishnah Sotah 7:8, probably this Agrippa). The believers, too, were Jews, and their meeting place was a Jewish home in Jerusalem. The chapter does not set Jews against Christians; it sets a ruler against God.
views.T: The church's prayer for Peter (12:5) became a model for prayer for imprisoned Christians and for church leaders. Tradition made this the moment Peter left for a long ministry elsewhere, in Catholic tradition for Rome (Eusebius; Jerome). James son of Zebedee is honored as the first apostle martyr (feast July 25 in the West, April 30 in the East), and the medieval pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela grew from a much later legend of his burial in Spain. 12:15 ("his angel") was cited for belief in guardian angels.

deep.h: Luke and Josephus on the death of Agrippa
deep.b:
Josephus, writing about AD 94, tells Agrippa's death in Jewish Antiquities 19.343–350. Set side by side:

  • Place: both, Caesarea. Josephus adds that it was at games held in honor of Caesar, in the theater.
  • Clothing: Luke, "royal clothes"; Josephus, a robe woven entirely of silver that glittered in the morning sun.
  • The crowd: Luke, "It's a god speaking, not a man!"; Josephus, flatterers called him a god and asked for his mercy.
  • His fault: Luke, "he did not give the glory to God"; Josephus, he did not rebuke them or reject their impious flattery.
  • The sign: Luke, an angel of the Lord struck him; Josephus, he saw an owl, which he had once been told would signal his death.
  • The death: Luke, eaten by worms; Josephus, violent pains in the belly, death after five days, aged fifty-four, in the seventh year of his reign.
  • Only in Luke: the quarrel with Tyre and Sidon and Blastus the chamberlain.

Most historians judge that the two writers drew on independent reports. The agreements are close where it matters, and the differences show the kind of detail each writer cared about: Josephus, the omen and the court; Luke, the angel of the Lord and the meaning of the event.

deep.h: Who was who: the Herods of the New Testament
deep.b: Readers often confuse them. Herod the Great (king 37–4 BC) rebuilt the temple and ruled when Jesus was born (Matthew 2). His son Herod Antipas (tetrarch of Galilee 4 BC–AD 39) beheaded John the Baptist and questioned Jesus (Luke 23:7–12); Manaen grew up with him (13:1). Herod the Great's grandson Herod Agrippa I (king AD 41–44) killed James and imprisoned Peter (Acts 12). Agrippa's son Agrippa II, with his sister Bernice, heard Paul's defense (Acts 25–26). Agrippa I's daughter Drusilla was the wife of the governor Felix (24:24).

settings.by: the church in Jerusalem, gathered in the house of Mary (12:12)
settings.when: during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, while Peter is in prison awaiting trial after James' execution
settings.why: The church has no political power against a king; it prays, and keeps praying through the night. Luke does not give the words, only their intensity. The prayer is answered more fully than those praying expect.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, many of whom knew of believers in prison, the scene says that prayer is the church's strength against rulers, and that God hears it.

settings.to: Peter, asleep between two soldiers in prison
settings.when: the night before Herod meant to bring him out, during the Feast of Unleavened Bread
settings.why: Short commands (get up, belt, sandals, cloak, follow) that move a sleeping, bewildered man out of prison step by step. They echo the Passover command to eat dressed for the road (Exodus 12:11).
settings.readers: Luke's readers hear a new Passover rescue: the God of the Exodus still brings his people out.

settings.when: just after the angel leaves him outside the prison
settings.why: Peter's realization gives Luke's verdict on the event: the Lord sent his angel and rescued him from the king and from the hopes of his enemies. It echoes Israel's rescues from Pharaoh.
settings.readers: Luke's readers hear the language of the Exodus and of the Psalms of rescue applied to the church's leader.

settings.what: Peter's report and message to James
settings.to: the believers praying in Mary's house
settings.when: in the night, before he goes into hiding
settings.why: Peter tells how the Lord brought him out and sends word to James and the brothers. Many read the message as handing leadership in Jerusalem to James, the Lord's brother, who leads there later in the story (15:13; 21:18); others think James already led beside the apostles, or that Luke only signals his importance.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the message introduces James, who later leads the mother church.

settings.what: Herod's public speech and the crowd's cry
settings.by: Herod Agrippa I; then the crowd
settings.to: the delegation from Tyre and Sidon and the people gathered at Caesarea
settings.when: on a set day at Caesarea, AD 44; Josephus says during games held for Caesar
settings.why: The speech, whose words Luke does not record, was a royal display to settle a dispute with the Phoenician cities. The crowd's flattery, calling him a god, was the kind of honor rulers in the Greek East often received. Herod's acceptance of it, not the speech itself, brings judgment.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, living under emperors who received divine honors, the story showed that God alone is to be worshiped and that rulers who claim his glory fall, while his word keeps growing.
views: Herod is struck by an angel of the Lord for not giving God the glory.
Herod failed to reject impious flattery; an owl signaled his death; he died after five days of pain (Jewish Antiquities 19.343–350).

title: A light for the nations
sum: While the leaders of the church at Antioch are worshiping and fasting, the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul. With prayer and the laying on of hands they send them off. On Cyprus they preach in the synagogues and reach the Roman governor, Sergius Paulus, in spite of a Jewish magician named Bar-Jesus or Elymas. Saul, "who also went by Paul," strikes the magician blind for a time, and the governor believes. From here on Luke calls him Paul, and Paul leads.

At Antioch near Pisidia, in the highlands of central Turkey, the synagogue leaders invite the visitors to speak after the readings. Paul's sermon, the longest of his that Luke gives, tells Israel's story from the Exodus to David, names Jesus as David's promised heir, and proves his resurrection from Psalm 2, Isaiah 55 and Psalm 16: through him comes forgiveness, and everyone who believes is justified. The next Sabbath almost the whole city comes. Some of the Jews oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas announce that they are turning to the Gentiles, quoting Isaiah's "light for the nations." Many Gentiles believe, but the apostles are driven out, shaking the dust from their feet.
readings: Read as history

Luke's details fit what is known of the region: Cyprus was governed by a proconsul, the Sergii Paulli are known from inscriptions, Pisidian Antioch was a Roman colony with a Jewish community, and synagogue worship included readings from the Law and the Prophets followed by teaching. Paul's letters confirm that he worked in Galatia, preached first to Jews and then to Gentiles, and met fierce opposition. How closely the sermon matches what Paul said that day is debated, as for all the speeches in Acts.
Read as Luke's model sermon to Jews

Peter's Pentecost speech opened the mission to Israel (chapter 2), Stephen's speech marked Jerusalem's rejection (chapter 7), and this sermon opens Paul's mission. It is Luke's example of how the good news was preached in a synagogue: Israel's history as God's gift, David's line fulfilled in Jesus, the Scriptures proving the resurrection, forgiveness offered, and a warning from the prophets. Paul's speeches later in Acts to Gentiles (14:15–17; 17:22–31) and to Christian leaders (20:18–35) complete the set.
Read as a story of election and response

The chapter begins with God choosing ("set apart for me," 13:2), recalls God choosing Israel's fathers (13:17) and David (13:22), and ends with Gentiles who "had been assigned to eternal life" believing (13:48), while others "judge themselves unworthy" (13:46). Readers in every century have asked how God's choice and human response fit together; the chapter holds both.

views.H: The journey began about AD 46. Cyprus was a senatorial province under a proconsul from 22 BC. Pisidian Antioch, a colony of Augustus settled with veterans and dominated by the imperial cult, had a Jewish community and Gentile sympathizers. Inscriptions show that women of rank held influence in such cities (13:50). Ramsay argued that Paul's route followed the proconsul's family connections; this remains possible but unproved.
views.C: Scholars debate the speeches in Acts. Some, following Martin Dibelius, think Luke composed them, as Thucydides admitted ancient historians did (History 1.22), to show what was fitting; others think they preserve the substance of early preaching. This sermon's Pauline features (justification, 13:38–39) are taken by Vielhauer as un-Pauline and by others as a fair summary for synagogue hearers. The reference to 450 years (13:20) and Saul's forty years (13:21) reflect Jewish chronology of the time.
views.L: The sermon has three parts, each marked by an address: "Israelites, and you who fear God" (13:16), "Brothers, sons of Abraham's family" (13:26), "So, brothers" (13:38). It moves from history to Jesus to appeal. The scene that follows repeats in miniature the pattern of Luke-Acts: Jesus' sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–30) also began with Scripture read in a synagogue, won admiration, then provoked anger when it mentioned God's grace to outsiders, and ended with the preacher driven out of town.
views.J: Jewish readers note how Jewish the sermon is: it tells Israel's sacred history, appeals to the Davidic promise and uses Jewish ways of linking texts (the shared word "holy" joining Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10). The opposition comes from "the Jews" of one synagogue, stirred, Luke says, by jealousy or zeal; but many Jews also believe (13:43; 14:1). Scholars such as Jacob Jervell argue that Acts shows Israel divided over Jesus, not rejected. Others, such as Jack T. Sanders, read Luke's portrait of Jews as increasingly hostile. Later Christian use of 13:46 to justify contempt for Jews is a misuse of a scene in which Paul's next step is another synagogue (14:1).
views.T: The sending at Antioch (13:1–3) has been read as a pattern for commissioning missionaries and, in many churches, for ordination with fasting, prayer and laying on of hands. The verse "as many as had been assigned to eternal life came to believe" (13:48) became a classic text in debates over predestination between Augustine's heirs, Calvinists and Arminians. The Orthodox and Catholic liturgical tradition draws on 13:2's "serving the Lord" (leitourgountōn) for the word "liturgy."

deep.h: Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch: how it is built
deep.b:
1. God's history with Israel (13:16–25). God chose the fathers, made the people great in Egypt, brought them out, bore with them in the wilderness, gave them Canaan, judges, Saul, and then David, "a man to suit my heart." From David's offspring God has brought a Savior, Jesus, to whom John the Baptist pointed.

2. What happened to Jesus (13:26–37). Jerusalem's people and leaders did not recognize him and fulfilled the prophets by condemning him; Pilate executed him; he was buried; God raised him and he was seen by many witnesses. Three Scriptures prove it: Psalm 2:7 ("You are my son"), the Greek of Isaiah 55:3 ("the holy things of David") and Psalm 16:10 ("your holy one" will not see decay). David died and decayed; Jesus did not.

3. The offer and the warning (13:38–41). Forgiveness of sins through him; everyone who believes is justified; beware the scoffers of Habakkuk 1:5.

The sermon closely parallels Peter's speech at Pentecost (2:14–40), which also uses Psalm 16 and the argument from David's tomb, and Stephen's survey of Israel's history (7:2–53). In 1967 John Bowker suggested the sermon follows the form of a synagogue homily built on the day's readings, perhaps Deuteronomy 4 and 2 Samuel 7; the idea has found some support but cannot be proved.

Luke switches names at 13:9 and never looks back, except when Paul retells his call (22:7, 13; 26:14). It is not a conversion name: Saul had been a believer for over a decade. Like many Jews in the Roman world he had two names, a Hebrew one, Sha'ul, after Israel's first king from his tribe of Benjamin, and a Latin one, Paulus, natural for a Roman citizen. Luke makes the change at the moment Paul confronts a magician before a Roman governor named Paulus and takes the lead from Barnabas ("Paul and the men with him," 13:13; "Paul and Barnabas," 13:43). From then on Paul is usually named first, though Barnabas comes first again at 14:14 and 15:12, 25. The new name marks the start of his mission among the Gentiles, the people whose language it belongs to.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two Sauls in one chapter
deep.b: Luke stops calling the apostle "Saul" at 13:9, and twelve verses later his sermon names the only other Saul in the New Testament: "Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin," whom God "removed" so that David could be raised up (13:21–22). The first Saul hunted David, God's anointed; the second persecuted the followers of David's greater son (9:4). I suggest Luke placed the name change and the sermon side by side on purpose: the Benjaminite Saul who opposed God's anointed gives way, and in his place stands Paul, servant of David's heir. Commentators have noticed the irony of Paul naming his namesake in the sermon; the deliberate pairing is my suggestion.

echoes: Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 1:31; Deuteronomy 7:1; 1 Samuel 13:14; Psalm 89:20; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 2:7; Isaiah 55:3; Psalm 16:10; Habakkuk 1:5; Isaiah 49:6; Luke 2:32; Luke 4:16–30; Matthew 10:14; 2:14–40; 7:2–53; 18:6; 28:25–28; Romans 1:16; Galatians 2:16

settings.by: the Holy Spirit, probably speaking through one of the prophets
settings.to: the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (13:1)
settings.when: while they were serving the Lord and fasting, about AD 46
settings.why: The word set apart two of the church's leaders for a mission whose goal is not yet named ("the work I have called them to"). It turned Antioch from a receiving church into a sending one.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, the mission that founded their churches began with a word from God to a praying church, not with a human plan.

settings.by: Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit
settings.to: Bar-Jesus (Elymas), a Jewish magician in the proconsul's circle, in the proconsul's presence
settings.when: at Paphos, as Elymas tries to turn Sergius Paulus away from the faith
settings.why: The words expose a false prophet and announce a temporary blindness. They show the governor that the God Paul preaches is stronger than the magic of his court. Like Peter's rebuke of Simon (8:20–23), it is a judgment meant to protect a new believer and perhaps to bring the offender to repentance ("for a time").
settings.readers: Luke's readers, in a world full of magic, learn that the gospel defeats sorcery and that Rome's officials found nothing to fear in it.

settings.what: Paul's sermon in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
settings.to: the Sabbath congregation of the synagogue: "Israelites," that is Jews and proselytes, and Gentile "God-fearers" who attended without converting
settings.when: on a Sabbath, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets, when the synagogue leaders invited the visitors to give "a word to encourage the people" (13:15)
settings.why: Paul speaks as a fellow Jew to people who know the Scriptures. He tells Israel's story as God's acts of grace leading to David, presents Jesus as the promised son of David whom God raised from the dead, and offers forgiveness and justification to all who believe, Jew and God-fearer alike. Knowing the audience matters: the sermon assumes the Scriptures and the hope for David's heir, and its warning from Habakkuk is aimed at people who might scoff at what God is doing in their own day. The God-fearers, addressed twice (13:16, 26), would hear that they could belong fully without circumcision.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, this was the model of how the gospel was first preached to Jews and God-fearers, and a reminder that their faith grew out of Israel's history and Scriptures.
views: A summary of what Paul said
Many scholars (Bruce, Hemer, Keener) think the speech gives the substance of Paul's synagogue preaching, shaped by Luke.
Others (Dibelius, Haenchen, Pervo) think Luke wrote it as a model sermon, following the practice of ancient historians (Thucydides 1.22).
John Bowker proposed that it follows the form of a homily on the day's readings.

settings.what: Paul and Barnabas announce the turn to the Gentiles
settings.to: the Jews of the synagogue who opposed them, before the crowd of the city
settings.when: on the following Sabbath, after the opponents contradict and insult Paul
settings.why: The words declare that the apostles had rightly offered God's word to Israel first, and now, rejected by these hearers, would take it to the Gentiles. They claim Isaiah 49:6 as their mandate: the Servant's mission to be a light for the nations. It is a statement about this city, not a final verdict on Israel; in the next city they go straight to the synagogue (14:1).
settings.readers: For Luke's largely Gentile churches the scene explained how they had come in, and grounded it in Israel's own prophet.

traditions.q: "As many as had been assigned to eternal life came to believe" (13:48). Does God choose who will believe, or does his choice rest on his foreknowledge of their free response?
views: God's election is unconditional: from eternity he chose some to eternal life, not because he foresaw their faith, and faith is the fruit of that election. Calvin read 13:48 as showing that faith depends on God's eternal choice (Westminster Confession 3.5–6; Canons of Dort 1.7–9).

God's eternal election in Christ is a cause of the salvation and faith of his children, and so 13:48 is a comfort; but there is no election to damnation, and those who are lost are lost by their own refusal. How both are true is left a mystery (Formula of Concord, article 11).

God predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037). In his eternal plan he includes each person's free response to grace (Catechism 600), and the Council of Trent rejected the view that the grace of justification is given only to the predestined (Session 6, canon 17). Within Catholic theology, Thomists and Molinists still debate how grace and freedom fit.

The Greek fathers read predestination in the light of God's foreknowledge: God foresees who will freely respond to his grace and predestines them to glory. Salvation is a cooperation (synergy) of God's grace and human freedom.

Election is conditional: God has decreed to save all who believe, and his grace enables every person to respond. John Wesley rejected unconditional election as making God the author of unbelief (Predestination Calmly Considered).

Divided. Particular (Reformed) Baptists hold unconditional election (Second London Confession, chapter 3); General and Free Will Baptists hold conditional election; the Baptist Faith and Message calls election God's gracious purpose "consistent with the free agency of man" (article 5).

title: Taken for gods
sum: At Iconium the pattern repeats: preaching in the synagogue, many Jews and Greeks believing, opposition stirring the Gentiles, a long stay with signs and wonders, a city split in two, and a plot to stone the apostles, who flee to Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd, shouting in their own language, decides that Zeus and Hermes have come down. The priest of Zeus brings bulls and garlands to sacrifice. Barnabas and Paul tear their clothes and rush into the crowd: they are only human, and they bring good news of the living God who made everything, who has always given rain and harvests as a witness to himself.

Then opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, win over the crowd, and stone Paul, dragging him out of the town for dead. He gets up and goes back in, and the next day leaves for Derbe. After making many disciples there, Paul and Barnabas retrace their steps, strengthening the believers, warning that the kingdom of God is entered through many troubles, and appointing elders in each church with prayer and fasting. They sail home to Antioch and report how God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
readings: Read as history

Lystra was a Roman colony in the Lycaonian highlands, where a local language and local cults survived; inscriptions from the region link Zeus and Hermes, and Ovid's legend of the two gods visiting Phrygia shows the story was told in the area. Paul's letters confirm a stoning (2 Corinthians 11:25), sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (2 Timothy 3:11) and miracles among the Galatians (Galatians 3:5).
Read as the gospel meeting the pagan world

Lystra is the first time in Acts that the apostles speak to Gentiles who know nothing of Israel's Scriptures. Paul does not quote the prophets; he starts from creation, the rain and the harvest, and calls people from "empty things" to the living God. The scene foreshadows Athens (17:16–34) and shows both the danger of being misunderstood and the way the gospel had to be translated for people of another world.
Read as a church planting manual

The second half of the chapter shows what Paul and Barnabas did after the first preaching: they returned to strengthen the new disciples, taught them to expect suffering, appointed elders, prayed and fasted, and entrusted them to the Lord. Missionaries and church planters have long read 14:21–23 as a pattern.

views.H: Iconium (modern Konya), Lystra and Derbe lay in the southern part of the Roman province of Galatia. Lystra and Pisidian Antioch were Roman colonies. The crowd's language, Lycaonian, is otherwise little known. Lystra was Timothy's home (16:1), and he may have witnessed these events (2 Timothy 3:10–11). The journey ends about AD 48, before the council.
views.C: Scholars note Luke's parallels between Peter and Paul (the healings of 3:1–10 and 14:8–10) and ask whether Luke shaped the story to match. The Lystra speech, like the Areopagus speech, is seen by some as Luke's own composition of a typical Jewish-Christian appeal to Gentiles; others find the same themes in Paul's letters (1 Thessalonians 1:9–10; Romans 1:19–23). That Luke calls Paul and Barnabas "apostles" only here (14:4, 14) is often taken as a trace of a source.
views.L: The chapter mirrors chapter 13: success, opposition, flight. The Lystra scene is a comic reversal of the Herod story (12:21–23): Herod accepted the cry that he was a god and died; Paul and Barnabas refuse divine honors and nearly die anyway at the hands of the same fickle kind of crowd. The return journey and report (14:21–28) close the first journey in a ring with 13:1–3.
views.J: Paul and Barnabas react to being worshiped as any faithful Jew would, with horror (tearing their clothes). Their speech is the Jewish case against idolatry, known from the Wisdom of Solomon (13–15) and from Jewish missionary writing, that the one Creator God is known from his works. The opponents who follow Paul from Antioch and Iconium are synagogue members who saw his teaching as a threat; Luke reports their violence frankly, but Jews also believe in Iconium (14:1), and Timothy's Jewish mother Eunice was from this region (16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5).
views.T: The church fathers admired the apostles' humility at Lystra. 14:22 ("through many troubles") became a watchword for Christian endurance, and 14:23 a key text in debates about church order: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican writers read it as apostolic ordination, Reformed and Free Church writers as election by the congregation (see the card on this page).

deep.h: Lystra: the gospel and folk religion
deep.b:
The people of Lystra were not philosophers. They believed the gods walked the earth and must be honored when they came; a local legend, told by the Roman poet Ovid, said Zeus and Hermes had once visited the region in disguise, and that those who failed to welcome them were destroyed. When a man lame from birth leaped up at Paul's word, the crowd drew the obvious conclusion and fetched the priest of Zeus.

Paul's answer is the first sermon in Acts to people with no knowledge of Israel's Scriptures. He does not quote a prophet. He starts with what they know: rain, harvest, food and good cheer. The God who made heaven and earth and the sea has never left himself without a witness. In the past he let the nations go their own ways; now he calls them from "empty things" (the word for idols) to himself. The same outline appears at Athens (17:22–31) and in Paul's letters (1 Thessalonians 1:9; Romans 1:19–23). It barely worked: the crowd that wanted to sacrifice to Paul one day stoned him the next.

On the way home Paul and Barnabas "chose elders for them in each church" (14:23). These were not men with long Christian experience; the churches were months old. They were probably older, respected members, perhaps Jewish believers who knew the Scriptures, given responsibility for teaching and care. The model was the synagogue and town, which were led by elders, and the Jerusalem church, which had elders by now (11:30).

Paul's letters to these churches, if Galatians was written to them, mention those who teach the word (Galatians 6:6) but not elders. Later letters speak of elders and overseers as the same office (Titus 1:5–7; Acts 20:17, 28). How this grew into the threefold ministry of bishops, presbyters and deacons, attested by Ignatius of Antioch about AD 110, is one of the main questions dividing the churches' views of ministry.

deep.h: The route of the first journey
deep.b: Antioch in Syria → Seleucia (port) → by sea to Salamis on Cyprus → overland to Paphos → by sea to Perga in Pamphylia → up into the highlands to Pisidian Antioch → Iconium (about 90 miles east) → Lystra (about 20 miles south) → Derbe (some 60 miles farther) → back through Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch → Perga → Attalia → by sea to Antioch in Syria. From Derbe the shortest way home was east through the Cilician Gates past Paul's home city, Tarsus; they chose instead to return through the cities where they had been attacked.

echoes: 3:1–10; 12:21–23; 17:22–31; 13:1–3; 15:3–4; 15:12; 16:1–2; Exodus 20:11; Psalm 146:6; Genesis 8:22; Psalm 147:8; Jeremiah 5:24; Isaiah 35:6; 2 Corinthians 11:25; Galatians 3:5; Galatians 6:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; 2 Timothy 3:10–11; Romans 1:19–23

settings.to: a man lame from birth, listening to Paul preach at Lystra
settings.why: Seeing the man's faith, Paul calls him to stand. The word is a command and a gift, like Peter's in 3:6, and it opens the way to the crowd's misunderstanding.
settings.readers: Luke's readers see that Paul acts with the same power as Peter, by the same Lord.

settings.by: the crowd of Lystra, in Lycaonian
settings.to: one another, about the two visitors
settings.when: just after Paul healed the man lame from birth
settings.why: The crowd hails Barnabas and Paul as Zeus and Hermes come down in human form, as local legend said those gods once had. Because they cried out in their own language, which the visitors did not speak, Paul and Barnabas grasp what is happening only when the priest arrives with bulls (14:14).
settings.readers: Luke's readers, many of them former worshipers of the gods, see how easily a miracle could be misread, and why the apostles had to point past themselves.

settings.to: the crowd of Lystra, Lycaonian-speaking country people and townsfolk, and the priest of Zeus with his bulls and garlands
settings.when: as the priest prepares to sacrifice to them as Zeus and Hermes, after the healing of the lame man
settings.why: The words were meant to stop a sacrifice at once and to redirect the crowd's awe from two men to the living God. With hearers who knew no Scripture, the apostles appeal to creation, rain and harvest, and to their shared humanity. Knowing the audience explains why this speech has no Old Testament quotations and no mention of Jesus in the part Luke reports: it is a first word to pagans.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Theophilus and the churches Luke wrote for, many of them former worshipers of the gods, the scene showed how far they had come and that the God of Israel had been caring for them all along.

settings.what: The apostles' teaching to the new disciples
settings.to: the new believers at Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch
settings.when: on the return journey, a few months after the churches were founded, in towns where the apostles had been attacked
settings.why: Young churches facing hostility needed to know that suffering was not a sign of failure. The teaching strengthened them to stay in the faith by telling them in advance that the road into God's kingdom runs through troubles.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who also faced suspicion and persecution, heard the same word addressed to them.

settings.to: each of the new churches, and the elders chosen for them
settings.when: on the return journey, with prayer and fasting
settings.why: Leaving the churches without their founders, the apostles provided leaders and entrusted them to the Lord. It gave each congregation local oversight on the pattern of synagogue and Jerusalem church.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, whose churches were led by elders, this showed that their leadership went back to the apostles' own practice.
views: Paul and Barnabas appointed the elders, perhaps with the church's agreement (most commentators).
The verb's old sense, "elect by show of hands," and 2 Corinthians 8:19 suggest the churches voted, with the apostles presiding (Calvin, many Free Church writers).

settings.what: The report to the church at Antioch
settings.to: the gathered church at Antioch that had sent them
settings.why: The missionaries give an account to the church that sent them. Their theme is what God has done and the door of faith opened to the Gentiles, which sets up the question of chapter 15: on what terms do Gentiles enter?
settings.readers: Luke's readers learn that mission is the work of the whole church, sent out and reporting back.

traditions.q: Paul and Barnabas "chose elders" in each church with prayer and fasting (14:23). Who should choose and set apart a church's ministers, and is ordination a sacrament?
views: Holy Orders is a sacrament given by a bishop through the laying on of hands and the prayer of consecration, in succession from the apostles. The apostles' appointing of presbyters in Acts is read as part of that line (Catechism 1536–1538, 1573, 1576).
Ordination (in Greek cheirotonia, the very word of 14:23) is a holy mystery performed by a bishop, with the people's assent voiced in the acclamation "Axios!" ("He is worthy!").

Bishops ordain priests and deacons by the laying on of hands according to the Ordinal; no one may minister publicly unless lawfully called and sent by those with public authority in the church (Thirty-Nine Articles 23 and 36).

No one should publicly teach or administer the sacraments unless he is rightly called (Augsburg Confession, article 14). The call comes through the church; ordination by prayer and laying on of hands is the public confirmation of that call.

Calvin argued that the Greek word shows the elders were chosen by the votes of the people, with Paul and Barnabas presiding (Institutes 4.3.15). In Presbyterian order, congregations elect their elders, who are then ordained by the session or presbytery; ordination is not a sacrament.

Each congregation chooses its own pastors (elders) and deacons. The Second London Confession says an elder is chosen "by the common suffrage of the Church itself" and set apart "by Fasting and Prayer, with Imposition of hands of the Eldership" (chapter 26.9). Ordination recognizes a call; it confers no grace.
